videos.title: How To Build The Future: Paul Graham & Amjad Masad
videos.description:
Replit was building toward the AI coding era years before it had a name. In 2024, the company shipped an agent that could take a request in plain English, work through errors, provision its own infrastructure, and keep going until the software actually worked. The model companies even reached out to ask how Replit had pulled it off.

Co-founder and CEO Amjad Masad had been thinking about making programming radically more accessible since 2008, and Replit’s original pitch deck predicted AI-generated code before the Transformer paper was published. Today, that same technology is moving into banks, manufacturers, and other large companies, where Amjad says teams are replacing software projects once scoped at $10 million with $250,000 of Replit.

On How to Build the Future, Paul Graham sits down with Amjad to talk about why Replit was so well positioned when coding agents arrived, what comes after vibe coding, and his bigger vision for the “self-driving company,” where AI agents increasingly build and operate the software a company needs.

videos.title: What the Top Companies Do Differently With AI Coding - Martin Harrysson & Prakhar Dixit, McKinsey
videos.description:
Martin Harrysson and Prakhar Dixit of McKinsey, with their colleague Shilpa, share what they're seeing across large companies using AI agents in software development. Most still report modest gains, but roughly the top 20 to 25% are now seeing 2x end-to-end improvements. They walk through what those companies do differently: shorter agent-driven cycles instead of two-week sprints, smaller pods with merged roles, curated skills and shared context, and change management that goes beyond pilots. They also cover why quality can drop as code generation speeds up, how the bottleneck moves to requirements and release, and why measuring impact is still the hardest part.

videos.title: A Model For Everyone: How Ronak From Trajectory Is Building Products For Continual Learning
videos.description:
Today’s agents are stuck in what Ronak Malde calls “pseudo continual learning”: intelligent, but updated in offline batches, like a paper road map you can’t reroute mid-trip. Ronak, co-founder of Trajectory, explains why closing that loop is the next learning paradigm, and why training your own model, which used to take a dedicated research team, months of work and hundreds of millions in compute, is now something a company can do in a few clicks with their own data. He details two research bets they are making available to everyone with their product: 1) a variant of GRPO that removes the need for a simulated environment by learning from single real-world rollouts instead of 16 replays of the same task, and 1) a meta-grader that increased data efficiency by 100x. Ronak explains how Harvey trained a model six times cheaper than frontier, improving an open-source baseline by over 4x on Harvey's own legal benchmark. He defines the difference between continual learning and recursive self-improvement and predicts product builders will become gardeners, setting trellises for products that grow themselves.

Hosted by Pat Grady and Lauren Reeder, Sequoia Capital

0:00 – Introduction
0:45 – Pseudo continual learning: paper maps vs Google Maps
2:48 – Do we need new architectures? Rich Sutton, David Silver, and the missing layer
4:33 – From a $100M consulting model to a product: lessons from SWE-1 at Windsurf
7:36 – Harvey: 6x cheaper than frontier, 4% to 18% on its own benchmark
8:55 – Why "Trajectory": the unit of work is a task, not a token
10:13 – The primitives of continual learning: traces, replayable environments, reward
12:56 – Group Size 1 and the meta-grader: training without an environment or a labeled reward
16:16 – The platform: train, eval and deploy in one click, and who it's for
18:58 – Rogo and intelligence density
20:14 – What's next: curiosity, and why continual learning beats RSI on alignment
24:19 – Research and product under one roof, and the product builder as gardener
27:26 – Why work at Trajectory, and the optimistic case: from 1% to 99%

videos.description:
As frontier AI labs expand into applications, where should startups build? a16z Partner Joe Schmidt joins HubSpot co-founder and CTO Dharmesh Shah to explore why the software opportunity is growing, and how founders can stay off the “Yellow Brick Road” the labs are racing down.

Drawing on HubSpot’s evolution, Dharmesh explains why founders should start with a narrow market, learn quickly, and solve the whole customer problem. They discuss where application companies can build lasting value as models become infrastructure: workflows, customer context, and the systems where work happens.

They also explore HubSpot’s AI experiments, the rise of one-person businesses, and why cheaper software creation could unlock markets that previously couldn’t support a software company.

videos.title: David Silver and Lasse Espeholt of Ineffable Intelligence: A Superlearner for the Age of Experience
videos.description:
David Silver spent two years building AlphaGo on human data. When he removed human data altogether building AlphaGo Zero, the AI surpassed AlphaGo in under two days. He left DeepMind to run that same bet in pursuit of superintelligence. David and Lasse Espeholt, co-founders of Ineffable Intelligence, explain their plan to build a “superlearner”—an agent that starts knowing nothing and discovers science, mathematics, and language for itself by direct experience instead of through a pre-training run. Silver argues that human-language reasoning is a ceiling, not a foundation, that alignment via chain-of-thought monitoring is already reaching its limits, and that the science of how superintelligences coexist should be worked out in simulation before anything touches the real world. Espeholt describes the GPU cluster and the lineage from IMPALA and SEED RL that makes the experiment possible. Silver’s forecast: strong evidence within a year, superintelligence in three.

Hosted by Sonya Huang, Sequoia Capital

videos.title: AI Realism Workflow the Pros Use (Eleven v4 + Seedance 2.5)
videos.description:
Keep your AI film characters sounding the same in every scene with Eleven v4 and Seedance 2.5.

Create AI Films → https://elevenlabs.io/creative?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=trend_tutorials&utm_content=create_consistent_character_voices_with_eleven_v4_and_seedance_2_5_ai_workflow

One of the biggest problems in AI filmmaking is characters losing their voice between scenes. In this workflow, we walk through how to pair Eleven v4 voice generation with Seedance 2.5 inside ElevenCreative so your character keeps the same voice, emotion, and delivery across every shot. We start by generating the perfect delivery in Eleven v4 using audio tags to direct the performance, then storyboard the scene in Flows with the voice over in place before generating any video.

From there we cover three ways to use that voice generation as a reference in Seedance 2.5, each one making the result more consistent:

• Method 1 • Use the Eleven v4 generation as an audio reference alongside a character reference and a set reference, then prompt the scene with tagged references
• Method 2 • Convert the MP3 into a plain black MP4 video and use it as a video reference, which tends to extract the delivery more reliably than the audio file
• Method 3 • Add a timestamp transcript from the black video using an LLM node, tag it in your prompt, and offset the timestamps so the action (like a crash landing) lands before the character starts speaking

We also cover choosing a voice from the Great voices for Eleven v4 selection in the voice library, lip syncing the generation to your character in Flows, and generating the scene separately so you can control the background. By the third method you can focus entirely on the prompt and the action while the voice delivery stays consistent every time.

videos.title: Confronting Our AI Future: Closing Keynote "Discovery Loop" with Jeff Dean and Fei-Fei Li
videos.description:
This closing fireside chat brings together two of the field's most consequential builders — Jeff Dean, whose work at Google has helped define the modern AI stack, and Fei-Fei Li, whose case for human-centered AI has shaped how the field thinks about who this technology should actually serve. Coming at the end of a day spent grappling with AI's risks and unresolved questions, the conversation turns to where the two of them agree, where they don't, and what they think the choices ahead really come down to.

*Speakers:* 

- Fei-Fei Li: Inaugural Sequoia Professor in the Computer Science Department at Stanford University, and a Founding Director of HAI. She served as the Director of Stanford’s AI Lab from 2013 to 2018. Li has served as a Vice President at Google and Chief Scientist of AI/ML at Google Cloud (2017-2018), board member or advisor in various public or private companies and is currently a Co-founder/CEO of World Labs, an AI company focusing on Spatial Intelligence and generative AI. 

- Jeff Dean: Computer scientist and software engineer. He is best known for his work at Google, which he joined in 1999. He led Google AI from 2018 to 2023 and was Google's chief scientist from 2023 to 2026. Dean co-founded the AI research start-up Discovery Loop in 2026.

videos.title: Fireside Chat with the Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering
videos.description:
The Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering is awarded to engineers responsible for innovations of global benefit to humanity. Past laureates include the inventors of the internet and the World Wide Web, the creators of GPS, and, closer to home, Fei-Fei Li alongside Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and Jensen Huang for their contributions to modern machine learning.

Stanford HAI Founding Director Fei-Fei Li, a QEPrize Laureate, and former Stanford University President John Hennessy, a QEPrize Trustee, discuss what sustains engineering breakthroughs in the age of AI, from open innovation to preparing the next generation. The conversation was moderated by Lord Vallance of Balham, Chair of the QE Prize's Trustee Board.

This event was held on October 7, 2026 at Stanford University.
